nodes.name: On a schedule
nodes.description: Starts the scenario at a fixed time or interval.
nodes.summary: Starts the scenario at a fixed time or interval.
nodes.body: The trigger for work that is not started by a message: a nightly reconciliation, a daily stock check, an hourly export. It connects to nothing and fetches nothing — its Poll times ARE the scenario’s schedule, and the step after it does the work. It emits one item carrying the moment it fired, which a later step can use to stamp a row or bound a query.

wizard.prompt: On a schedule — every hour, day or week

inputs.label: Poll mode
inputs.options: Every Minute · Every Hour · Every Day · Every Week · Every Month · Every X minutes · Custom (Cron)
inputs.hint: How often the scenario is checked. This is the scenario’s schedule.
inputs.description: How often the scenario runs. This IS its schedule — choosing a mode writes it, and the fields that appear depend on the mode. Every Day at 9am unless you change it, because a scenario that runs every minute by default would run before anybody had finished building it.

inputs.label: Hour
inputs.hint: 24-hour clock, in the trigger timezone.
inputs.description: Shown for the daily, weekly and monthly modes: the time of day the poll runs, on the 24-hour clock in the trigger timezone.

inputs.label: Minute
inputs.description: Minute of the hour for the scheduled modes, or the interval length for Every X minutes.

inputs.label: Weekday
inputs.options: Sunday · Monday · Tuesday · Wednesday · Thursday · Friday · Saturday
inputs.description: Shown for the weekly mode: which day the poll runs. Sunday through Saturday, matching how the schedule is stored.

inputs.label: Day of the month
inputs.hint: 1 to 31. A month without that day is skipped.
inputs.description: Shown for the monthly mode: which day of the month the poll runs, 1 to 31. A month without that day is skipped rather than shifted.

inputs.label: Cron expression
inputs.hint: Five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.
inputs.description: Shown for the custom mode: five fields — minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.

outputs.description: When this run started, as an ISO timestamp.
The same moment in milliseconds, for arithmetic.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Schedule.RunAt}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: On webhook call
nodes.description: Starts the scenario when another system calls its URL.
nodes.summary: Starts the scenario when another system calls its URL.
nodes.body: The trigger for work that somebody else sets off: an order placed in a storefront, a job finishing in SAP, a form submitted on a site you do not own. It connects to nothing and fetches nothing — it hands the scenario whatever arrived, as Body, Headers and Query. The URL is created on this node and can be read again whenever you need it; rotating it issues a new one and stops the old one working. Only a PUBLISHED scenario can be called, so the URL is live when you publish and dead when you unpublish.

wizard.prompt: When another system calls us

inputs.label: Method
inputs.hint: Which request this URL answers. Anything else is refused.
inputs.description: Which request this URL answers, POST or GET. POST is what most systems send and carries a body; GET is what a monitor or a simple ping uses. A request using the other one is refused, so the URL cannot be run by accident from a browser address bar unless you chose GET.

inputs.label: Reply with
inputs.hint: Sent the moment the call is accepted, before the scenario finishes.
inputs.description: What the caller is told the moment the call is accepted. 202 Accepted is the truth — the run is queued, not finished — and a well-behaved sender will not retry on it. Choose 200 OK only for a sender that treats anything other than 200 as a failure, which some older systems do.

inputs.label: Ignore link previews and crawlers
inputs.hint: Stops a chat or ticket that merely shows the URL from running the scenario.
inputs.description: Whether to refuse link preview crawlers. Pasting the URL into a chat or a ticket makes that tool fetch it to draw a preview, and without this the fetch runs the whole scenario and is billed like any other run. On unless you have a reason.

inputs.label: Security and extras
inputs.description: The settings most webhooks never need, kept behind a chooser so the panel shows the two or three controls that matter to everybody. Adding one reveals its field; removing it clears the setting as well as the row, so a rule can never go on applying invisibly.

inputs.label: Only accept calls from
inputs.hint: Comma-separated addresses. Behind a proxy, TRUSTED_PROXIES must name it or every caller looks like the proxy.
inputs.description: Which callers are accepted, by address. Empty means any — the unguessable token in the URL is what makes the endpoint private, and this narrows it further to known senders, which is worth doing when the caller is one fixed server. Exact addresses only: a range that matches subtly wrongly either admits callers you excluded or refuses the one you meant to allow, and both look like the setting working, so a range is refused rather than guessed at.

inputs.label: Require these headers
inputs.hint: A call without them is refused. For a sender that proves itself with a shared secret rather than the URL.
inputs.description: Headers a call must carry, name and value, or it is refused with 403. The unguessable token in the URL is already this endpoint's credential, so this is for the sender whose own rules say otherwise — a platform that signs with a header, or a policy that forbids secrets in URLs. Values are compared in constant time and never appear in a refusal, which goes to whoever called, right or wrong.

inputs.label: Accept file uploads
inputs.hint: Lets a form or a system post files. Each arrives as an attachment named after its form field, so a later step can send or read it. Off by default. A file costs storage, and is kept only as long as the run that received it.
inputs.description: Whether a call may carry files. Off by default: a webhook that accepts them stores every one it is sent, which costs storage and is not what most senders are doing. On, a multipart form post is accepted and each file arrives as an attachment named after its form field, so Send a message can attach it and Convert to File can read it with nothing in between. Off, such a call is refused with 415 rather than quietly read as text, which would produce boundary markers that look like data. A stored file lives exactly as long as the run that received it: when that run leaves the history window the file goes with it, so storage follows the same window as everything else rather than growing for ever.

inputs.label: Also receive the raw body
inputs.hint: Adds Raw — the body exactly as sent. Needed to check a signature from GitHub, Stripe or Shopify in a Code step.
inputs.description: Adds Raw to this node's output: the body exactly as it arrived, beside the parsed Body. Needed to check a signature — GitHub, Stripe and Shopify all sign the original bytes, and parsing and re-serialising a body changes them, so the signature over the rebuilt text never matches. A Code step does the comparison, which is why no provider is named here and every one of them works. Off by default: it doubles what each run stores.

outputs.description: What the caller sent. An object for JSON or a form; the raw text for anything else.
The request’s headers, lowercased. Authorization and Cookie are removed.
Values from the URL’s query string, if any.
The body exactly as sent, when "Also receive the raw body" is on. Absent otherwise.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Body}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

Body.example: Send a first call to see your own fields here.

nodes.name: On form submitted
nodes.description: Starts the scenario when somebody submits the form at its link.
nodes.summary: Starts the scenario when somebody submits the form at its link.
nodes.body: The trigger for work a person sets off: a delivery request, a leave application, a site visit booked by a customer. You write the questions here and the page is built from them, so there is no screen to design and nothing to host. The link is created on this node and can be read again at any time; it works only while the scenario is published, so unpublishing takes the form down. Anybody holding the link can submit — it asks for no account — which makes the link itself the thing to share carefully.

wizard.prompt: When somebody fills in a form

inputs.label: Form address
inputs.hint: The end of the link, after your organisation’s name. Leave it empty to take it from the title. Changing it after you have shared the link breaks the old one.
inputs.description: The readable part of the link, after your organisation’s name. Empty means it comes from the title, which is almost always what you want. Worth setting by hand when the title is long, or when you want the same address kept after rewording the heading — and worth NOT changing once the link is out, because every copy of it stops working. Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens: a link read out on the phone or typed from an email cannot carry capitals or spaces.

inputs.label: Form title
inputs.hint: Shown at the top of the page.
inputs.description: The heading at the top of the page, and the first thing somebody reads. Write what you are asking them to do rather than naming the system: "Request a delivery" tells them why they are here, "Delivery form v2" does not.

inputs.label: Text under the title
inputs.hint: Optional. Use it to say who should fill this in, or what happens next.
inputs.description: Optional text under the title. The useful things to put here are who should be filling this in, what happens after they submit, and anything they need to have to hand before they start.

inputs.label: Fields
inputs.description: The questions, in the order they appear. Each has a label, a type, and whether it must be answered. The label is how a later step reads it — `Email` is Form.Email. Two questions may not share a label, and publish refuses the form until they do not. A text box can show a placeholder. A choice needs options, and can be a menu or buttons, one answer or several. A password is stored as [redacted] on the run; the live steps still receive it. Content is text on the page and not an answer. Hidden travels with the submission and is not shown.

inputs.label: Button label
inputs.description: The words on the button that submits. "Submit" is fine; naming the action is better, as in "Request delivery", because somebody who hesitates at a button reads it twice.

inputs.label: After submit
inputs.options: Show a message · Go to a web address
inputs.hint: What the person sees the moment their answers are accepted.
inputs.description: What the person sees the instant their answers are accepted — not when the scenario finishes, which may take a while and may fail. A message keeps them on the page; a web address sends them somewhere of yours. Either way they get an answer, because a form that submits and shows nothing is one people fill in twice.

inputs.label: Message
inputs.defaultValue: Thank you. We have got your answers.
inputs.hint: Shown in place of the form once it is submitted.
inputs.description: Shown in place of the form once it is accepted. Say what will happen next rather than only thanking them, so they know whether to expect a reply and roughly when.

inputs.label: Security and styling
inputs.description: The settings most forms never need, kept behind a chooser so the panel shows the questions rather than a wall of controls. Adding one reveals its field; removing it clears the setting as well as the row, so a rule can never go on applying invisibly.

inputs.label: Custom styling
inputs.hint: Change any line to restyle the page. These are the only names the page relies on, so your styling survives changes to our markup.
inputs.description: The look of the public page, as a block of named variables rather than free-hand CSS. Change a line — the button colour, the width, the font — and the page follows; the variables are the only names it relies on, so your styling is not broken the next time our markup changes. It is loaded as a stylesheet on your form only, and the page refuses anything that is not styling.

inputs.label: Only accept submissions from
inputs.hint: Comma-separated addresses, for a form only one office should reach. Behind a proxy, TRUSTED_PROXIES must name it or every visitor looks like the proxy.
inputs.description: Which visitors may submit, by address. Empty means anybody holding the link, which is the normal case for a form sent to customers. Worth setting when the form is internal and reached from one office or one VPN. Exact addresses only, for the same reason the webhook gives: a range that matches subtly wrongly either admits people you excluded or refuses the ones you meant to allow, and both look like the setting working.

inputs.label: Web address
inputs.hint: They are sent here as soon as the form is accepted.
inputs.description: Where to send them once the form is accepted. Use it when you already have a page of your own that says what happens next, or when the form is one step of a longer journey on your site.

outputs.description: The answers, one property per question, under its label.
When the form was submitted.

nodes.name: Get Data/Inputs
nodes.description: Reads spreadsheet rows by path or all sheets.
nodes.summary: Reads spreadsheet rows by path or across all sheets.
nodes.body: Use this as the first node when a spreadsheet is the source of truth. It resolves the spreadsheet, reads the sheet you name, and emits one bundle per row — so every node after it runs once per row, up to the limit you set.

wizard.prompt: Rows from a spreadsheet

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: Which spreadsheet to work on. The ID Finder lists the ones this connection can see, so you never paste a raw ID.

inputs.label: Sheet Name
inputs.description: The tab inside the spreadsheet to read.

inputs.label: Table contains headers
inputs.description: When Yes, the header row supplies field names for the mapping picker instead of column letters.

inputs.label: Return
inputs.hint: Which end of the sheet the limit applies to. Last rows is the newest appended rows when the sheet grows downward.
inputs.description: First rows returns from the top of the data (below the header). Last rows returns the final rows on the tab — use that when you want the most recently appended records.

inputs.label: Limit
inputs.hint: Maximum number of rows returned per run.
inputs.description: Maximum rows returned per run. Keep it low while testing; raise it once the downstream nodes are configured.

outputs.description: The row, keyed by the sheet’s own header names.
Sheet row number, used to write a status back later.

nodes.name: Add a row
nodes.description: Appends a new row to the selected sheet.
nodes.summary: Appends a new row to the selected sheet.
nodes.body: Writes one row per incoming bundle at the bottom of the sheet. Field values usually come from mapped tokens of earlier nodes, so a five-column sheet takes five mapped values.

wizard.prompt: Add a row to a spreadsheet

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: The spreadsheet being written to.

inputs.label: Sheet Name
inputs.description: Tab that receives the new row.

inputs.label: Table contains headers
inputs.description: When Yes, values are matched to header names rather than column order.

inputs.label: Values to Send
inputs.hint: One row per column you want to write. Leave empty to map the whole item by header name.
inputs.description: One row per column to write. The Column finder lists the sheet’s own headers, so a value lands where you meant it. Each value takes a fixed string or an expression. Left empty, the node matches the incoming item’s Sheet_Data against the header row instead — which is how it behaved before this field existed.

outputs.description: Sheet row number of the appended row.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Row_Number}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: Create a spreadsheet
nodes.description: Creates a new spreadsheet file in Google Drive.
nodes.summary: Creates a new spreadsheet file in Google Drive.
nodes.body: Makes the FILE, not a tab — this is the node that has no Spreadsheet ID to ask for, because it produces one. Map Spreadsheet.Id into a later node to write into what it just made. A freshly created spreadsheet may not appear in your Sheets file list until it has been opened once, so the Url output is the quickest way to see it.

inputs.label: Title
inputs.hint: Name of the new spreadsheet file.
inputs.description: Name of the new spreadsheet file. Google allows duplicates, so this is not checked.

outputs.description: ID of the new file, which later nodes paste into their Spreadsheet ID.
Title it was created with.
Direct link to open it.
Name of the tab it starts with.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Spreadsheet.Id}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: Delete a spreadsheet
nodes.description: Moves a whole spreadsheet file to the Drive trash, or removes it for good.
nodes.summary: Moves a whole spreadsheet file to the Drive trash, or removes it for good.
nodes.body: Removes the FILE and every sheet in it — the most destructive node in the catalog, and the only one that needs Drive write access, so a connection authorised earlier is asked to reconnect. Move to trash is the default and stays recoverable for thirty days; Delete permanently keeps no copy anywhere, and neither Drive nor this product has an undo. The title is read before the removal so the run log can name what went rather than only its ID.

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: The spreadsheet FILE to remove, with every sheet inside it.

inputs.label: What to do
inputs.description: Move to trash is reversible for thirty days. Delete permanently is not reversible at all.

outputs.description: ID of the file that was removed.
Title it had, read before the removal.
True when it went to the trash and can still be restored.
True when it was removed for good.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Spreadsheet.Id}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: Create a sheet in a spreadsheet
nodes.description: Adds a new sheet (a tab) inside a spreadsheet that already exists.
nodes.summary: Adds a new sheet (tab) to an existing spreadsheet.
nodes.body: Adds a tab INSIDE an existing spreadsheet — it does not create a new spreadsheet file, which is why it asks which document to add to. The new tab will not appear in your Google Sheets file list; open the spreadsheet you named and it is there alongside the others. Creates one per run, so it suits a per-month or per-run tab that later nodes write into. A duplicate title is refused rather than created: Google allows two tabs with the same name, which would leave any later delete-by-name ambiguous.

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: The existing spreadsheet that receives the new tab. This node does not create a spreadsheet file — it adds a sheet to one you already have.

inputs.label: Title
inputs.hint: Name for the new sheet. Must not already exist in this spreadsheet.
inputs.description: Name for the new sheet. Refused if the spreadsheet already has one by this name.

outputs.description: Title of the sheet that was created.
Numeric sheet id Google assigned, which addresses the tab in later calls.
Position of the tab within the document.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Sheet.Title}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: Delete a sheet from a spreadsheet
nodes.description: Removes one sheet (a tab) from a spreadsheet. The file itself is kept.
nodes.summary: Removes a sheet (tab) from a spreadsheet by name.
nodes.body: Deletes one tab and everything on it, so it is the one Sheets node worth reading twice before publishing. The spreadsheet FILE is untouched — only the sheet inside it goes. The name must match exactly; when it does not, the error lists the tabs the document actually has rather than reporting a bare failure. Deleting the last remaining sheet is refused, because a spreadsheet must keep one.

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: The spreadsheet holding the sheet to remove. The file is kept; only the named tab is deleted.

inputs.label: Sheet to delete
inputs.hint: Exact tab name. The node lists what the document does have if this is not found.
inputs.description: Exact name of the tab to remove. Case and spacing must match what Google holds.

outputs.description: Title of the sheet that was deleted.
Numeric id it had.
True once Google has accepted the removal.

nodes.outputNote: Downstream maps as {{N.Sheet.Title}} where N is this step's 1-based position.

nodes.name: Update a row
nodes.description: Updates an existing row by its row number.
nodes.summary: Updates an existing row by its row number.
nodes.body: Overwrites values in a row you identify — most often with the Row_Number output of an earlier Get Data node. Use it to write a status back after a downstream system accepted or rejected the record.

wizard.prompt: Update a row that already exists

inputs.label: Spreadsheet ID
inputs.description: The spreadsheet being updated.

inputs.label: Sheet Name
inputs.description: Tab that contains the row.

inputs.label: Table contains headers
inputs.description: When Yes, values are matched to header names rather than column order.

inputs.label: Row number
inputs.hint: Leave blank to use the Row_Number of the incoming item.
inputs.description: Which sheet row to write, counting from the top including the header. Blank uses the incoming item’s Row_Number, which is what Get Data/Inputs emits — set it only when running this node without one upstream.

nodes.name: OCR — Extract text
nodes.description: Reads text from PDFs, scans and images.
nodes.summary: Reads text from PDFs, scans and images.
nodes.body: The entry point for any document flow. It takes a file — usually an attachment from a preceding email node — and returns machine-readable text that later nodes parse, classify or prompt over.

inputs.label: Source
inputs.options: Attachment from previous node · File URL · Uploaded file
inputs.description: Where the file comes from: an upstream attachment, a URL, or a file uploaded to the workspace.

inputs.label: Accepted file types
inputs.options: PDF, PNG, JPG · PDF only · Images only
inputs.description: Files outside the accepted set are skipped instead of failing the run.

inputs.label: Language
inputs.description: Recognition language. Auto-detect handles mixed-language documents; naming a language raises accuracy on noisy scans.

inputs.label: Pages
inputs.hint: Leave as All to OCR every page.
inputs.description: Page selection, e.g. All or 1-3. Restricting pages cuts run time on long PDFs.

inputs.label: Output format
inputs.description: Plain text emits one text blob; Structured JSON keeps page and block coordinates for downstream field extraction.

outputs.description: Machine-readable text recognised from the file.
Number of pages processed.

nodes.name: Extract structured fields
nodes.description: Pulls named fields from invoices, POs and forms.
nodes.summary: Pulls named fields from invoices, POs and forms.
nodes.body: Returns one value per named field, each with a confidence score. Fields that score below the threshold follow the low-confidence rule instead of silently reaching downstream systems — which is what keeps bad values out of SAP.

inputs.label: Document type
inputs.options: Invoice · Purchase order · Delivery note · Receipt
inputs.description: Selects the extraction profile. Each type ships with its own field vocabulary and layout expectations.

inputs.label: Fields to extract
inputs.hint: Comma-separated field names the model should return.
inputs.description: Comma-separated field names the model should return. Each becomes a mappable token for later nodes.

inputs.label: Model
inputs.options: Extraction v2 · Extraction v1 · Custom model
inputs.description: Extraction model version. Custom model uses the profile trained on your own documents.

inputs.label: Confidence threshold
inputs.description: Minimum score a value must reach to pass through. 0.80 is a reasonable default for printed invoices; raise it for financial postings.

inputs.label: On low confidence
inputs.options: Flag for review · Skip record · Stop scenario
inputs.description: What happens to values under the threshold: hold them in the review queue, drop the record, or stop the run.

outputs.description: Object of extracted field values, keyed by field name.
Lowest confidence score across the extracted fields.

nodes.description: Converts document tables into rows.
nodes.summary: Converts document tables into rows.
nodes.body: Detects the table on the page and emits an array of rows, one bundle per line item. Pair it with a spreadsheet Add a row node to turn a scanned delivery note into structured data.

inputs.label: Table hint
inputs.description: A phrase near the table that helps locate it when a page holds several tables.

inputs.label: Columns
inputs.hint: Column names in the order they appear in the document.
inputs.description: Column names in document order. Extra document columns are ignored; missing ones come back empty.

inputs.label: Merge multi-page tables
inputs.description: When Yes, a table continuing on the next page is stitched into one result instead of two.

Number of rows extracted.

nodes.summary: Labels each document by type before routing.

inputs.description: The candidate labels. Keep them mutually exclusive — overlapping labels lower confidence.

inputs.description: Classification model version.

nodes.name: AI prompt / summarize

nodes.summary: Runs a prompt over extracted document text.

inputs.label: Input

nodes.name: Extract with instruction
nodes.description: Runs your instruction and schema against any input and returns JSON, XML or text.
nodes.summary: Runs your instruction and schema against any input and returns JSON, XML or text.
nodes.body: A general-purpose extraction node: you supply the service URL, API key and model name, write the instruction in plain language, and declare the shape of the result. Whatever the instruction and schema describe is what the node returns — the schema drives the fields, the output format decides how they are serialised. Unlike the fixed Document AI profiles, nothing here is tied to a document type, so the same node handles invoices, contracts, emails or raw API text.

inputs.label: Service URL
inputs.hint: The MUNTQ Intelligence endpoint this node calls.
inputs.description: The MUNTQ Intelligence endpoint the node posts to. Point it at your own deployment when self-hosting.

inputs.label: API key
inputs.description: Key sent as the bearer credential. Stored with the scenario and masked in the field.

inputs.label: Model name
inputs.description: Model identifier passed through to the service, e.g. a tuned extraction model for your document set.

inputs.label: Input source
inputs.options: PDF attachment from previous node · Text from previous node · Document text · Raw payload · File URL
inputs.description: Where the content comes from. "PDF attachment from previous node" renders the pages of the attachment to images and lets a vision model read them, which is the path for scanned or mixed-language documents. The others take an upstream text value, OCR document text, a raw payload, or a file URL the service fetches itself.

inputs.label: Input
inputs.hint: What the instruction runs against — usually an upstream text or OCR output.
inputs.description: The exact value the instruction runs against. Insert an upstream token so each run carries real content.

inputs.label: Instruction
inputs.defaultValue: Extract the invoice header and totals. Use null when a value is not present.
inputs.description: Plain-language description of what to extract and how to treat missing or ambiguous values. This is the main control: the more specific the instruction, the more stable the result.

inputs.label: Output schema
inputs.description: Declares the fields and their types. The service returns exactly these keys; each one becomes a mappable token for downstream nodes.

inputs.label: Enforce schema strictly
inputs.description: On, the node fails when a field cannot be produced in the declared type. Off, unresolved fields come back null and the run continues.

inputs.label: Temperature
inputs.description: Response randomness. Keep it near zero for extraction so repeated runs agree.

inputs.label: Max tokens
inputs.description: Upper bound on the response. Raise it for large schemas or long line-item tables.

nodes.name: SAP System
nodes.description: Lists or writes records by selecting an OData service, entity set, and operation.
nodes.summary: Reads, creates and changes records in any OData service the connected SAP system publishes.
nodes.body:
Asks the system what it has rather than offering a fixed list: the pickers read the Gateway catalogue and then the chosen service, so a custom Z-service is available the moment it is registered. Stores the service and entity set names, so a saved scenario runs without reopening a picker. Execute the step once to give the mapping panel real fields — the output shape belongs to the entity set, not to this node.

Reading fetches the collection once however many items reach this step; creating and changing run for each item, so three items are three records. A change sends only the fields in the body and leaves the rest alone, and is refused if the record moved in SAP since this step read it — which is a conflict somebody should see rather than overwrite.

nodes.name: Create Record
nodes.description: Posts a new record into an SAP module.
nodes.summary: Posts a record to a service on the connected SAP system.
nodes.body:
Writes a document — sales order, journal entry, goods receipt — to a service on the connected SAP system. It fetches a CSRF token with the session it belongs to, posts the record, and returns what SAP answered — one item per row. The step fails when SAP refuses the request. A service that answers 200 while reporting that nothing was created says so in its own fields: check that field with an If after this step. Posting is not reversible from here, so test against a development client first.

Use SAP System to create a record in a collection the catalogue lists; use this when the path is already known — a service registered outside the usual namespace, one the catalogue does not carry, or an address built from a value an earlier step produced.

inputs.description: Selecting anything other than None reveals that scheme’s credential fields below.

inputs.label: Method
inputs.description: HTTP verb sent with the request. GET and DELETE send no body, so the body fields are not offered for them; PATCH is there for the APIs that update a record in place rather than replacing it.

inputs.label: URL
inputs.description: Endpoint to call. Mapped tokens may be embedded in the path or query string.

inputs.description: The parts of a request most calls do not need — query parameters, headers, and the full response envelope. Each is inert until added.

inputs.hint: How long this call may take. 30 seconds suits a normal API. The longest wait is 120 seconds, and each page of a paged read gets its own.
inputs.description: How long to wait for the call before it fails. A hung endpoint otherwise holds a worker until the whole run is cancelled. Each page of a paged read is timed on its own.

inputs.hint: Follow next link walks @odata.nextLink or d.__next on a GET and returns one item per record across the pages. It stops at the page limit.
inputs.description: No sends one request. Follow next link keeps requesting while the body carries @odata.nextLink or d.__next, and emits one item per record across those pages. GET only. A full-response request stays a single call, because the envelope is the point of that option.

inputs.label: Query parameters
inputs.hint: Appended to the URL and encoded for you, so a mapped value with a space or an & lands intact.
inputs.description: Rows appended to the URL as query parameters, encoded for you. A repeated key is kept rather than replaced, so ?id=1&id=2 is expressible, and a parameter already written into the URL is left alone.

inputs.label: Headers
inputs.hint: Accept and Content-Type are set to application/json when you set neither.
inputs.description: Repeatable header rows. Add item appends a row; the bin icon removes one. Accept defaults to application/json when you set none, because an OData service otherwise answers with Atom XML whose records sit four levels down.

inputs.label: Return the full response instead of the data
inputs.hint: Off: one item per record, mapped directly. On: one item carrying the status, headers, cookies and body — needed for a CSRF token handshake.
inputs.description: Off, the output is the response DATA: one item per record, so a collection can be iterated and a field is mapped by its own name. On, the output is one item carrying Request and Response — status code, headers, cookies and body — which is what a CSRF handshake needs and what every mapping written before this change expects. Response.Headers carries set-cookie as an array for parity with other tools, but Response.Cookies is the one to map into a Cookie header: the raw values carry path, HttpOnly and Expires attributes, and a server rejects a cookie sent back with them in a way that looks like an authentication failure.

nodes.name: Run code
nodes.description: Transforms data with custom JavaScript or Python.
nodes.summary: Transforms data with custom JavaScript or Python.
nodes.body: For the logic no other node covers: reshaping bundles, computing totals, merging fields, filtering records. The script receives the items from the preceding node and must return items — what it returns becomes the input of the next node. It cannot touch the file system or make HTTP calls; use the HTTP Connector node for requests.

wizard.prompt: Reshape the data with a piece of code

inputs.label: Mode
inputs.options: Run Once for All Items · Run Once for Each Item
inputs.hint: All Items runs the script once per execution; Each Item runs it once per incoming bundle.
inputs.description: All Items executes the script once per run and gives you the whole batch; Each Item executes it once per incoming bundle.

inputs.label: Language
inputs.description: JavaScript runs in an isolated sandbox. Python runs in its own process. Neither can read files or call the network; use the HTTP node for requests.

inputs.label: JavaScript
inputs.hint: Built-ins use the $ prefix: $input, $json, $node. Promises and console.log are supported.

inputs.description: Shown when Language is Python. Built-ins use the _ prefix — _input, _items, _item — and items take bracket access: item["json"]["field"].

nodes.name: Router / Conditional Branching
nodes.description: Splits the flow using if-else conditions.
nodes.summary: Splits the flow using if-else conditions.
nodes.body: Creates two labelled routes on the canvas. Each route carries its own nodes and runs only when its conditions evaluate to true — the standard way to send low-confidence documents to a human while the rest post automatically.

wizard.prompt: Send the whole batch down one of several paths

inputs.label: Routes and conditions
inputs.description: Each route is a lane under the router with its own insert button, and carries its own rows of left value, operator and right value. Left values are usually mapped tokens; click a Map chip to insert one. Operators: is equal to, contains, exists. Add AND Rule requires every condition in a group; Add OR Rule passes when any group matches. A route with no rules always runs.

nodes.outputNote: Pass-through or unknown shape — map from a recorded run, not from declared paths.

nodes.name: If
nodes.description: Tests each item and sends it to the true or false branch based on configured conditions.
nodes.summary: Sends the items that match down one branch and the rest down the other.
nodes.body: Two branches, true and false, and every item goes down exactly one of them — so "email the unpaid orders, archive the rest" is one node and two lanes rather than two filters with opposite settings. Different from the router, which asks the question once and sends the whole bundle one way; different from the filter, which drops what does not match instead of giving it somewhere to go. A branch that receives no items is marked skipped, along with the nodes only it feeds.

wizard.prompt: Treat some items differently from the rest

inputs.label: Conditions
inputs.description: One row per comparison — a value, an operator and what to compare it with. The combinator after the first row decides whether every condition must hold or only one. With nothing configured every item is treated as matching, so the false branch stays empty.

nodes.outputNote: Pass-through or unknown shape — map from a recorded run, not from declared paths.

nodes.name: Join
nodes.description: Combines items from incoming branches and continues one shared downstream path.
nodes.summary: Brings every branch back together, so the flow continues as one.
nodes.body: Sits after a branching node and is fed by the last step of each of its branches, so "email the unpaid orders, archive the rest, then log all of them" is one chain rather than the same logging step duplicated on both sides. Its wiring is not drawn and cannot be edited: it is recomputed whenever the graph changes, so extending a branch keeps the join correct rather than leaving it pointed at a step that is no longer last.

nodes.name: Filter
nodes.description: Tests each item and keeps only matching items, or only items that do not match.
nodes.summary: Drops the items that do not match, and passes the rest on.
nodes.body: Different from the router: no lanes, no branches, just fewer items on the one path. Where the router asks "which way does the flow go", this asks "which of these items is worth continuing with". An empty result stops the branch the same way a trigger finding nothing does.

wizard.prompt: Keep only the items that matter

inputs.label: Conditions
inputs.description: One row per comparison — a value, an operator and what to compare it with. The combinator after the first row decides whether every condition must hold or only one. A filter written before this took a single comparison; that comparison appears as the first row and still runs.

inputs.label: Keep
inputs.description: Whether to keep the items that match, or the ones that do not.

nodes.name: Loop Over Items
nodes.description: Processes incoming items in configurable batches and exposes batch position metadata.
nodes.summary: Hands the items on in batches, counted and numbered.
nodes.body: Every step in a scenario already runs once per item, so iterating a list needs no node — wire the steps in a line. This exists for the two things that are not automatic: sending items onward in GROUPS, for an API that takes fifty records per call rather than one, and telling each batch where it sits in the run so a step can report "3 of 40" or act only on the last one. It draws no loop on the canvas and creates no cycle; the steps after it simply run once per batch.

wizard.prompt: Hand the items on a few at a time

inputs.label: Each batch holds
inputs.options: Each item on its own · A list of items
inputs.description: Each item on its own keeps the items as they are and only numbers them, which is the common case. A list of items puts the whole batch into Loop.Items on a single item, which is what a bulk endpoint needs.

inputs.label: Items per batch
inputs.hint: How many items travel together. 1 hands them on one at a time, which is what every step does anyway.
inputs.description: How many items travel together. One means one at a time. The count is capped at the number of items, so a batch size larger than the bundle produces a single batch rather than an empty one.

outputs.description: Which batch this is, counting from 1.
How many batches there are in total.
True on the final batch, for a step that should run once at the end.
The items in this batch, when the batch holds a list.

nodes.name: Wait
nodes.description: Pauses execution for a duration or until an approval link resumes the scenario.
nodes.summary: Pauses the scenario without holding a worker.
nodes.body: For a time releases the worker and continues after the duration, up to seven days. Until resumed emails one pair of links and continues when either is opened. The decision applies to every item that reached this step, so a batch of 10,000 is one pause and one answer, not 10,000 pauses. Put an If in front of it when only some batches need a person. Reject does not fail the run: the items continue with Approval.Decision set to rejected, and a later If can stop them.

wizard.prompt: Pause until a time, or until somebody approves

inputs.label: Wait
inputs.description: For a time continues on its own. Until resumed continues only when a person opens the link in the email.

inputs.label: Amount
inputs.description: How long to wait, together with the unit. The shortest wait is one minute and the longest is seven days.

inputs.label: Unit
inputs.description: Minutes, hours or days.

inputs.label: Email the decision links to
inputs.hint: One email, for the whole batch. Approving or rejecting continues every item that reached this step, up to 10,000.
inputs.description: Who receives the approve and reject links. The message is one email for the whole batch. If this deployment has no mail relay, the links are saved on the run so an operator can forward them.

inputs.label: Approval message
inputs.hint: Optional text shown with the approval links so the reviewer sees the business context, not just a generic prompt.

inputs.label: Fields to show
inputs.hint: Comma-separated fields from each item to display in the approval email and page. Leave blank to show the full JSON payload for each item.

outputs.description: approved or rejected, present only after somebody uses a decision link.

nodes.name: Split Out
nodes.description: Turns an array inside one item into one item per element.
nodes.summary: Turns an array inside one item into one item per element.
nodes.body: The node that makes a bundled response iterable. An API that answers with one object containing twenty rows arrives as ONE item, so a mapping can only ever reach the first row and a downstream node runs once instead of twenty times. Point this at the array and each element becomes its own item, which is what every per-item behaviour in the engine is built around.

wizard.prompt: Handle each line of a list separately

inputs.label: Field to split out
inputs.hint: Dotted path to the array. An OData reply usually nests it, e.g. d.results.
inputs.description: Dotted path to the array within the item, e.g. d.results. An empty result produces no items rather than an error.

inputs.label: Each new item holds
inputs.options: Only the element · Element and parent fields
inputs.description: Whether each new item is just the array element, or the element merged with the parent item’s other fields. Merging is how a line keeps its order number.

nodes.name: Edit Fields
nodes.description: Sets, renames or trims the fields on each item.
nodes.summary: Sets, renames or trims the fields on each item.
nodes.body: The most ordinary thing a scenario does, and until now it needed the Code node. Each row names a field and gives it a value — a fixed string, or an expression resolved against the item being processed. "Keep only the fields set here" turns a twenty-field API response into the three columns a sheet wants, without a script and without collapsing the bundle into one item.

inputs.label: Fields to set
inputs.description: One row per field. The value takes a fixed string or an expression; a row with an empty name is ignored.

inputs.label: Everything else
inputs.options: Keep all input fields · Keep only the fields set here
inputs.description: Whether the item keeps its other fields, or is reduced to exactly the fields named above.

nodes.description: Combines incoming items into one aggregate item, optionally collecting a named field.
nodes.summary: Combines many items into one.
nodes.body: The inverse of Split Out, and what a bulk endpoint needs. Thirteen items become one item holding thirteen values, so a create-many API is called once instead of thirteen times. Collect whole items, or one named field from each.

inputs.label: Aggregate
inputs.description: Whether to collect each item whole, or read one field out of every item.

inputs.hint: Dotted path read from each item.
inputs.description: Shown for One field. The dotted path read from each item.

nodes.name: Convert to File
nodes.description: Writes mapped rows to a CSV or Excel file, serializes JSON, or decodes base64 into a file.
nodes.summary: Turns items into a CSV, Excel or JSON file, or base64 text into a file.
nodes.body: Builds the file a person opens or a system imports, and carries it on the output item so Outlook and Gmail can attach it. Every item goes into one file by default — a report of what the scenario did. Pick, order and rename the columns here, and read rows straight out of a list inside an item, so a report needs no Edit Fields or Split Out in front of it. Base64 to file turns an encoded document from an API back into a real attachment, working out its type from the data. In a CSV, a cell that would start an Excel formula is written as text, because these files are built from what customers send.

wizard.prompt: Turn the result into a spreadsheet or CSV file

inputs.label: Operation
inputs.options: Convert to CSV · Convert to Excel · Convert to JSON · Base64 to file
inputs.description: CSV opens anywhere; Excel adds sized columns and a filter row; JSON is for another system to read; Base64 to file decodes an encoded document.

inputs.label: File name
inputs.hint: The extension is added for you. Map a value into it to name each run’s file.
inputs.description: The file name. The extension is added when it is missing, and a mapped value names each run’s file, e.g. SO-{{…}}.

inputs.label: Columns
inputs.hint: Blank: every field, in the order they appear. Type a field name such as salesOrder, or map a value.
inputs.description: Which columns, in which order, under which headers. Type a field name to read that field from every row — a row without it gets an empty cell — or map a value from an earlier step. Text that no row has as a field is written as it is, so a misspelt name shows up in the file rather than vanishing. Blank takes every field, nested ones as Record.Id-style columns.

inputs.label: Options
inputs.description: Settings most files never need. Each is inert until added.

inputs.label: Rows from a field
inputs.hint: A list inside each item. Every entry becomes a row — no Split Out needed.
inputs.description: A dotted path to a list inside each item, such as Intelligence.Json or d.results. Every entry becomes one row.

inputs.label: Delimiter
inputs.hint: Semicolon is what Excel expects in regions that write 1,5 for one and a half.
inputs.description: What separates the columns. Semicolon suits Excel in regions that use a comma for decimals.

inputs.label: Leave out the header row
inputs.description: Writes the rows only, for a system that expects no header.

inputs.label: Excel-friendly encoding (UTF-8 BOM)
inputs.hint: Turn on when Excel shows Arabic, Urdu or accented letters as symbols.
inputs.description: Adds the marker Excel needs to read UTF-8, so Arabic, Urdu and accented letters display correctly. Some import tools reject it, so it is off by default.

inputs.label: One file per item
inputs.hint: Off: every item goes into one file. On: each item gets its own, kept beside its data.
inputs.description: Each item gets its own file, kept beside the item’s own fields and files — one invoice PDF per order, say, rather than one report for the run.

inputs.label: Put file in field
inputs.hint: The name the file is carried under. Email nodes attach it by this name.
inputs.description: The binary field the file is stored under. Defaults to data; an email node’s attachment setting names it, or * for every file.

inputs.label: Base64 text
inputs.hint: The encoded file itself. A data: URL works too.
inputs.description: The encoded file itself, usually mapped from an API response. Standard or URL-safe base64, or a data: URL.
